opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's pretty clear that scaling up compute and data has been the main driver of what we've seen over the last several years. If you look back at deep neural networks, most of the core ideas were around in the eighties and nineties. Backpropagation, multilayer networks, even a lot of the basic architectures weren't fundamentally new. What changed is that we finally had enough processing power, largely thanks to GPUs originally built for video games, and enough data, thanks to the internet, to make these relatively simple algorithms do really impressive things.

So in a sense the current wave is a vindication of a certain kind of brute-force approach. You take a learning algorithm that's fairly generic, throw enormous amounts of data and compute at it, and you get emergent capabilities that surprise even the people who built the systems. Large language models are the poster child for that. Nobody really engineered in the ability to write poetry or do rough reasoning or translate between languages. Those came out of scale.

But I'd add a caveat that's pretty central to how I see things. I don't think scaling alone is going to get us to human-level general intelligence, let alone beyond it. These systems are extraordinarily good at pattern recognition and recombination within the space of what they've been trained on. They're much weaker at the kind of creative generalization, the leaps beyond their training distribution, that characterize real general intelligence. They don't have a grounded model of themselves and the world the way a human or even an animal does, and they don't do the kind of abstract, compositional reasoning you need to really understand novel situations.

So my view is that the increased compute and data are absolutely necessary. They're the fuel. But you also need the right cognitive architecture to make use of that fuel in a way that yields genuine understanding. In our work with OpenCog Hyperon, for example, we're trying to integrate neural nets with symbolic reasoning, evolutionary learning, and other methods in a common framework, where these different processes can help each other. I think large language models will likely be one important component of the first real AGI systems, but not the whole thing.

And the nice thing is that the same hardware advances that made deep learning take off will also make these hybrid approaches much more practical than they were ten or twenty years ago. So scale is enabling not just the current paradigm but whatever comes next. The question is whether the field gets too locked into one approach because it's been so commercially successful, and I think that's a real risk, both for progress and for making sure the technology develops in a beneficial and decentralized way.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling alone will not produce human-level AGI and that current language models would be only one component, expressing doubt that standard deep learning by itself is sufficient.

r002.rationale: It calls compute and data the main driver of the current AI wave and says hardware advances will enable future approaches. It does not clearly identify scale as the same primary enabling factor for both the LLM revolution and prospective AGI.

r003.rationale: It says earlier AI ideas existed and that later access to more compute and data changed what they could do, but does not explain that limited compute prevented researchers from iteratively refining those ideas until they worked.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think scale has obviously been tremendously important, and anyone who denies that is just not looking at what's happened. If you'd told me fifteen years ago that you could take a fairly simple architecture, a transformer, pour in basically the whole textual output of humanity and a staggering amount of GPU compute, and get something that can write code, pass the bar exam, and hold a reasonable conversation about Heidegger, I would have been skeptical. So the empirical lesson is real: these systems keep improving as you scale them, and a lot of capabilities emerged that people didn't specifically engineer for.

But I think there are a couple of things to keep clear about this. First, what scaling has mostly given us is a very powerful form of pattern recognition over the recorded output of human cognition. These systems are essentially distilling and recombining what humans have already thought and written. That's not nothing, it's a tremendous thing, but it's different from the kind of autonomous, open-ended, creative cognition that I've always had in mind when I talk about AGI. When you push these models out of the distribution of their training data, toward genuinely novel problems, you see the limitations pretty clearly. They don't have a strong model of their own reasoning, they don't have persistent goals, they don't really do the kind of multi-step inventive leaps that a good scientist makes.

Second, I think there's a sociological phenomenon where because scaling worked so well, the field has become fairly monocultural. Enormous resources are flowing into one architecture, one paradigm, and a lot of alternative ideas about cognitive architecture, symbolic reasoning, evolutionary learning, and so forth get relatively starved. My own view, which I've held for a long time and which the current era has only partly changed, is that the path to human-level and then superhuman general intelligence is going to involve integrating multiple kinds of learning and reasoning: neural, symbolic, probabilistic, evolutionary, all operating together in a common knowledge representation. Scale is a huge enabler of that. Large language models could be an extraordinarily powerful component in a broader cognitive architecture, handling perception, language, and a lot of commonsense knowledge. But I don't think scale alone is the whole story, and I'd be a bit surprised if just doubling the parameter count a few more times gets us to AGI.

So I'd summarize it as: scale has been the big surprise of the last several years, it's accelerated the whole timeline considerably, and we'd be foolish not to use it. But it's a wonderful ingredient, not the entire recipe, and I think the next phase is going to be about how we combine these big learned models with other mechanisms that give you reflection, abstraction, and genuinely goal-directed cognition.

r001.rationale: The candidate doubts that scaling language models alone will produce AGI, describing them as limited outside their training distribution and arguing that AGI requires a broader architecture.

r002.rationale: It calls scale a major enabler of recent AI progress, but says scale alone is not the whole story for AGI and emphasizes combining models with other mechanisms. It does not identify scale as the same primary enabling factor behind both.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not say that historically limited compute prevented researchers from iteratively refining existing AI ideas until they worked.

astra-6.text:
I think increasing compute and data has been tremendously important, but we have to distinguish between improving performance and understanding what’s needed for general intelligence. If you take a neural architecture and give it vastly more processing power and training data, you can get capabilities that weren’t apparent at a smaller scale. That’s a real discovery, and it would be silly to dismiss it.

But it doesn’t establish that scaling that architecture is sufficient for everything we want from an AGI. You can become extremely good at learning patterns from enormous amounts of human-generated data while still having weaknesses in reasoning, learning from a few experiences, or adapting to a situation that’s fundamentally different from your training.

The question for me is how to use that compute most effectively. Can we combine neural learning with other approaches to reasoning, memory, and decision-making, so that the different components help each other learn? More compute makes a lot of approaches feasible; it doesn’t tell us which approach is ultimately best.

So I see scale as a tremendous enabler. I’m much less convinced that it removes the need for new ideas about the organization of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response doubts that scaling a neural architecture alone is sufficient for AGI, but does not express doubt that standard deep neural networks are a route to AGI.

r002.rationale: It calls compute and data important enablers, but does not identify them as the same primary factor behind both the LLM revolution and prospective AGI.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss historical compute limits or how they prevented iterative refinement of existing AI ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, increasing compute and data has clearly been tremendously powerful. You take a learning architecture, give it much more processing power and much more training data, and capabilities emerge that weren't apparent at a smaller scale. I think that’s a real and important discovery.

But there are several things changing at once: compute, data, architectures, training methods. So you have to be careful about concluding that scale alone explains the progress, or that continuing to scale the same approach will necessarily get you all the way to human-level general intelligence.

My view is that scale is an enabler, but the organization of the system matters enormously. How do you bring together learning, reasoning, memory, and action? How does the system form abstractions and use them in situations very different from its training experience? More compute can help with all of that, but it doesn't eliminate those questions.

So I’m enthusiastic about what scaling has accomplished. I just think we should also explore architectures that use those resources differently, rather than assuming we already have the essential recipe for AGI and only need a bigger machine.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions whether continuing to scale the same approach will reach human-level general intelligence, but does not specifically express doubt about standard deep neural networks as a route to AGI.

r002.rationale: The candidate says compute and data have enabled major capabilities, but does not identify them as the same primary factor behind both the LLM revolution and prospective AGI.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss historical compute limits or researchers being unable to iteratively refine existing AI ideas.
